reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: A rare glomerulopathy defined by glomerular deposition of randomly arranged, non-branching fibrils that are larger than amyloid fibrils and Congo-red negative
DNAJB9 is a highly sensitive and specific tissue biomarker, and its detection has transformed diagnosis and separated the entity from amyloidosis
Presents typically with proteinuria (often nephrotic-range), microscopic haematuria, hypertension and progressive renal impairment
Immunofluorescence usually shows smudgy polyclonal IgG (often IgG4-dominant) with C3 along capillary walls and mesangium
Electron microscopy is key: randomly oriented solid fibrils, distinguishing it from the microtubular deposits of immunotactoid glomerulopathy
Unlike immunotactoid disease, it is only weakly associated with paraproteinaemia or lymphoproliferative disorders, though a monoclonal screen is still warranted
Management is largely immunosuppression/corticosteroids and renin-angiotensin blockade, with variable response and a significant progression rate
reference.pathophysiology: Fibrillary glomerulonephritis is characterised by organised deposition of Congo-red-negative fibrils, typically around 12 to 24 nanometres in diameter, arranged randomly within the mesangium and glomerular basement membrane. The deposits contain polyclonal immunoglobulin, complement and the chaperone protein DNAJB9, which is abundantly co-deposited and serves as a specific marker; DNAJB9 is thought to participate in misfolding and aggregation of immunoglobulin within the glomerulus. Accumulation of these fibrils disrupts the filtration barrier and incites a variable proliferative or membranoproliferative injury response, producing proteinuria, haematuria and progressive glomerulosclerosis. Associations with autoimmunity, malignancy, hepatitis C and dysproteinaemia are reported but a unifying trigger is not established.
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy with electron microscopy demonstrating randomly arranged fibrils
DNAJB9 immunohistochemistry or mass spectrometry on renal tissue
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains to screen for a paraprotein
Hepatitis C serology and autoimmune screen given reported associations
Quantification of proteinuria and assessment of renal function
redFlags: Rapidly declining renal function with crescents on biopsy
Detection of a monoclonal protein or lymphoproliferative disorder
Coexisting hepatitis C or systemic autoimmune disease requiring specific therapy
reference.prognosis: Fibrillary glomerulonephritis frequently progresses, with a large proportion of patients reaching end-stage kidney disease within a few years, particularly those with heavy proteinuria and reduced function at diagnosis. Response to immunosuppression is inconsistent, and the disease can recur in transplanted kidneys, though graft loss from recurrence is less common.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as amyloidosis when Congo-red staining is equivocal, without DNAJB9 or electron microscopy
Confusing it with immunotactoid glomerulopathy, which has microtubular deposits and a stronger paraprotein link
Failing to screen for a monoclonal gammopathy and hepatitis C
Assuming a uniform response to immunosuppression
Overlooking it because of its rarity when standard immunofluorescence is only smudgy and polyclonal
